title: David Dhawan Just Directed His Final Film. Varun Showed Up. So Did ₹27 Crore.
excerpt: The father-son dynasty that gave Bollywood its loudest comedies bows out with a rom-com that's fighting for survival in an OTT world — and somehow still filling seats.
body:
If you grew up watching Bollywood comedies in the '90s, you owe **David Dhawan** a debt of laughter. *Coolie No. 1*. *Hero No. 1*. *Haseena Maan Jaayegi*. *Partner*. *Bade Miyan Chote Miyan*. The man didn't just direct comedies — he codified an entire era of Hindi cinema where the punchline was the plot and nobody apologized for it.

<youtube></youtube>

And now, with **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai**, he's reportedly done.

The film — starring his son **Varun Dhawan**, alongside **Mrunal Thakur** and **Pooja Hegde** — opened on June 5 and pulled **₹27 crore nett in its first four days** at the Indian box office. By the standards of a mid-budget romantic comedy in 2026, that's not a disaster. By the standards of what the Dhawan name once commanded, it's a quiet goodbye.

The reviews were mixed to unkind. Critics called it familiar, with one noting, "It feels like a rehash of Dhawan's earlier works, lacking the freshness that once defined his films." The audience showed up anyway — not in the stampede numbers that once greeted the Govinda-David Dhawan blockbusters, but steadily, loyally, the way you show up for the last day of something you've loved for three decades.

Multiple trade reports have described *Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai* as David Dhawan's final directorial outing — a career spanning four decades, bookended by the 1980s and this: a comedy about a man caught between two women, which is roughly the plot of 60% of David Dhawan's filmography. He didn't reinvent himself at the finish line. He repeated his greatest hits one last time, with his own son leading the chorus. There's something both stubborn and deeply touching about that. It's a poignant full circle, with Varun embodying the very comedic spirit his father perfected, making this farewell feel deeply personal for the family and fans alike.

**Varun**, to his credit, knows how to sell this material. He's charming in the way actors are charming when they've grown up on film sets and absorbed comic timing through osmosis. He's never been better than when he's channelling **Govinda's energy** — the winks, the physical comedy, the shameless flirtation — a style he's clearly inherited and honed under his father's watchful eye, and *Hai Jawani* gives him plenty of room to do exactly that. **Mrunal Thakur** and **Pooja Hegde** bring their own screen presence to the triangle, making a well-worn setup feel warmer than it probably deserves to.

The opening tells the story in numbers. A ₹7.50 crore Friday. A flat Saturday. A 10% jump on Sunday to close the weekend at ₹24 crore. Then a ₹3.25 crore Monday — a 60% drop that trade analysts called "big." By Day 4, the film had cracked the **Top 10 highest-grossing Bollywood films of 2026**, which sounds impressive until you realize that the number-one film, *Dhurandhar 2*, sits at ₹1,186 crore. The gap between Bollywood's biggest hits and its mid-range films has never been wider. The middle class of Indian cinema — the ₹50–80 crore romcom — is an endangered species.

And the reason is sitting on your phone. The current 8-week OTT window means your audience knows that every theatrical film will be streaming soon. Why spend ₹500 on tickets when JioHotstar will have it before the monsoons hit? Trade analysts have been screaming about this for months: the OTT window is "directly undermining the theatrical business," conditioning audiences to simply wait.

For NRIs, the calculus cuts even deeper. Tickets in the US cost $15–$20. Showtimes at desi theatres are limited and inconvenient. And the diaspora knows — *knows* — that the film will be on streaming before anyone organizes a WhatsApp group to pick a date. The incentive to rush to a cinema for a romantic comedy, a genre that doesn't demand IMAX or Dolby Atmos, has evaporated. This shift not only impacts box office revenues but also affects remittances, as families abroad may choose to save on entertainment costs, further complicating the financial ties that bind them to their homeland. The nostalgia associated with Dhawan's films often serves as a cultural touchstone for NRIs, making this farewell particularly poignant.

Which is what makes this Dhawan goodbye bittersweet. David Dhawan built his career in an era when the only screen was the big one, and the only competition for a Friday release was another Friday release. His comedies were communal experiences — the kind you watched with an entire row
